newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE-KOLODKO FATE HANGS ON POLISH GVT REFORM.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-KOLODKO FATE HANGS ON POLISH GVT REFORM.

text.p: The rumour is back in Poland's parliament that Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko, seen widely as the guardian of budgetary restraint and lower inflation in three successive leftist cabinets, may soon be out of a job.

But even many of Kolodko's critics question whether the coalition dares to drop the assertive, non-party academic who has shaped Poland's economic strategy since taking his post, with the rank of deputy prime minister, in April 1994.

The ex-communist Democratic Alliance (SLD) and its smaller Peasant party (PSL) coalition partner are wrangling furiously over which should control key economic ministries after a reorganisation of central government due to start on October 1.

"Kolodko's fate depends on how ministries are shared out..., whether the finance ministry remains in SLD hands and whether the SLD nominates Kolodko," Peasant party parliamentarian Janusz Piechocinski told Reuters.
Asked about Kolodko's prospects, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told reporters last month that no minister could be sure of his position during the gradual reform.
But many are sceptical.
"This is the 21st version of Kolodko's departure and 20 times it hasn't happened," said Janusz Dabrowski, vice-president of the independent Gdansk-based Market Economy Research Institute.
Analysts and dealers said his departure might arouse concern abroad, where markets are attuned to political risk in emerging economies, though less so on domestic markets.

"If Kolodko's position is threatened, it would not be surprising if foreign investors were to start to withdraw short-term capital from the Polish market," said Jacek Lech, deputy chief dealer of Poland's Bank Handlowy SA.

Kolodko came in after the two coalition parties won September 1993 elections, partly with promises to moderate the hardships of market reforms adopted by Solidarity-rooted governments following the 1989 fall of communism.
These early reforms, steered by liberal finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz, had stabilised the economy after years of chaos and laid a basis for growth which resumed in 1992.
Kolodko set out a "Strategy for Poland" -- a first signpost of official policy with clear, if over-optimistic, medium to long-term goals of sustained growth and curbed inflation.
FROM COLD TURKEY TO SOARING EAGLE
Poland's transition since 1989 speaks for itself.
Last year it had Europe's fastest growth, of seven percent, and expects to sustain it at above five percent.
Exports are thriving, foreign investment has topped $10 billion, the private sector accounts for around 65 percent of Gross Domestic Product and unemployment is declining slowly.

In 1994 Poland agreed with foreign commercial creditors on its huge communist-era debt. Last year it won an investment grade rating of Baa3 from Moody's Investor Services and returned to international markets with a successful $250 million Eurobond.
A success for 47-year-old Kolodko has been Poland's invitation to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, a vital step towards the Holy Grail of European Union entry.
"Poland has transformed itself 'from cold turkey to soaring eagle'," Kolodko wrote in the preface to his updated economic strategy, "Package 2000", issued this year.

He resents arguments that Balcerowicz deserves the glory for Poland's transformation and, never guilty of false modesty, he gives more credit for his own plans than for his predecessor's laissez-faire philosophy.
"Kolodko is a master of economic propaganda, who skilfully sells his successes and hides failures," said Piechocinski.
One area of only limited success is controlling inflation.
In July it was at 20.4 percent -- well above the 17 percent target Kolodko had hoped to reach in December last year and which is now the goal for end-1996.

But Dabrowski praised Kolodko for managing to restrain leftist cabinet colleagues, hungry for still-faster growth and vote-grabbing spending, from the kind of financial course that took Hungary's inflation up to around 28 percent in 1995.

"Kolodko is a good guardian of state money -- he has not allowed a new explosion of inflation or an excessive increase in the budget deficit such as happened in Hungary," admitted Dabrowski, who has many reservations about Kolodko's record.
KOLODKO SOMETIMES CONTROVERSIAL
Some Kolodko tactics here have been controversial -- he has tried to get the central bank to cut official interest rates faster, in the hope of reducing inflationary expectations.
The independent bank resisted, concerned this tactic could backfire, leading to sharp exchanges last year between Kolodko and National Bank of Poland President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz.
Kolodko was forced into a compromise by the cabinet in April when he proposed a sharp cut in Poland's high tax rates.

His ministry's apparent slip up in granting tax breaks on personal donations, which are hard to police, cost the budget dearly this year and Kolodko's attempt to blame taxpayers for taking advantage of the loophole earned him sharp criticism.
Opposition critics say he should have done more to force the pace of privatisation, especially of banks, and vital social security reforms.
Kolodko, aligned with the SLD but not a member, is exposed, despite support from President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

The finance ministry's role is to be diminished during the coming reorganisation and it is not certain Kolodko will find a place in any of the new economic ministries. His dogmatic style and impatience has earned him many foes in parliament.
"His manner may be alright in academia, but in politics it brings enormous tensions in the cooperation with parliament and within the government," said PSL's Piechocinski.
But, apart from his international reputation, there are other grounds to expect Kolodko will survive in the cabinet.
The 1997 budget has yet to be steered any PSL politician, Kolodko would be our favourite," said the Gdansk institute's Dabrowski.
